video_title: AI’s third era: the rise of persistent AI coworkers | Tara Seshan (OpenAI’s product lead)
gist: Tara Seshan, OpenAI's product lead for ChatGPT work and Codex, argues AI products are entering a third era of persistent 'co-worker' agents after chat and coding-agent eras, and lays out the internal operating discipline (build for models 2-3 months out, be empirical not theoretical, elevate ambition) that produced Codex's recent momentum and OpenAI's plan to collapse ChatGPT/Codex/Work into one auto-routed interface.

themes.theme: The Three Eras of AI Products and New Work Primitives

insights.claim: OpenAI's product lead for ChatGPT work and Codex frames AI product evolution in three eras: era one was chat, era two is working with agents (mostly coding agents so far), and an emerging third era is persistent AI 'co-workers' that get things done alongside a person, potentially collaboratively with other humans.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan, OpenAI product lead for Codex and ChatGPT work
insights.so_what: Frames where OpenAI is positioning its roadmap next — watch for 'persistent co-worker' features (shared/multi-agent collaboration surfaces) as the next big product push beyond single-user agent chat.
insights.quote: If you think about the first era of AI products as chat, the second era of these products working with agents, that third era that might come soon is how do you work with a persistent co-worker who is able to get things done with you.

insights.claim: OpenAI's 'Sites' feature lets any user generate a shareable, database-backed, auto-updating mini web app from a single prompt (games, trip trackers, dashboards) without any deployment knowledge, and Seshan says it has replaced much of her daily use of docs and slide decks.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A concrete, underused feature turning natural-language prompts into hosted apps — signals OpenAI pushing beyond chat into lightweight app creation as a wedge against tools like Notion, and a data point for how quickly 'build software' becomes a mainstream, non-technical action.
insights.quote: Sites kind of realized the dream of like malleable personal software that Alan K[ay]... flagged in the in the 60s of like the true personal computer is one that has personal software.

insights.claim: Codex's '/visualize' command auto-generates charts and dashboards from a user's own data or usage history (e.g., 'visualize my ChatGPT usage'), turning raw activity data into presentation-ready visuals without manual chart-building.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Another concrete, low-awareness feature that compresses analytics/reporting work; useful signal for how OpenAI is embedding BI-style tooling directly into the agent rather than ceding that surface to dashboard vendors.
insights.quote: slash visualize is incredibly exciting

insights.claim: Seshan sees a 'cozy software' movement emerging where individuals build small AI-native apps for their friend group (e.g., a friend's app that turns any content into a personal podcast feed, and a private social network called GATS), enabled because AI now lets anyone build custom software for a tiny audience.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Early evidence of a long-tail 'software for five friends' category emerging from AI app-building tools — worth watching as a leading indicator of consumer AI-native app formats outside big platforms.

insights.claim: On mobile, ChatGPT's 'work' mode runs agent tasks in the cloud rather than locally, so a user can start a task, lose connectivity (e.g., on a subway), and return to a completed result — Seshan calls this an underappreciated, 'magical' element of the current product.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Cloud-native, disconnect-tolerant execution is a differentiator for agent products aimed at knowledge workers versus tools that require a persistent local session.

themes.theme: PM Craft and the Human Role in an Emergent AI Market

insights.claim: In static or slow-moving markets (e.g., payments), rigorous first-principles grand strategy is rewarded because outcomes are more predictable, but in the AI product market conditions are so emergent and fast-changing that being 'prolific and empirical' beats being 'academic and theoretical,' and staying tightly coupled to research progress is essential.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Explains why long-horizon strategic planning underperforms in frontier-AI product work — investors evaluating AI-product teams should weight iteration speed and empirical testing culture over polished roadmaps.
insights.quote: Being prolific and empirical is way more important than being academic or theoretical rather than writing out some long reasoning doc. Instead, it's like how do I get to something I can try out and test with users as fast as possible.

insights.claim: The unchanged core of the PM job, even in the AI era, is defining the single most essential hypothesis that determines whether a product works, testing it as fast as possible, and feeding results back into refining that hypothesis — most of the job's other 'trappings' (status docs, presentations) have become less important.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A durable filter for evaluating whether a product org is actually testing the right thing versus performing process; useful diligence question for teams building AI products.
insights.quote: What is like that specific most important thing to test and everything else like any other grand strategy you concoct is not relevant.

insights.claim: OpenAI's internal product discipline is to build for where models will be in two to three months, not for current model capability or a one-year-out projection — both of those horizons are described as 'equally wrong.'
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A concrete planning horizon investors can use to sanity-check AI-native product roadmaps: teams anchored too far behind or ahead of the model curve are structurally mispositioned.
insights.quote: You fail if you build for where the models are now. You fail if you build for where you think the models will be in a year. Both outcomes are equally wrong.

insights.claim: Kevin Weil, OpenAI's then chief product officer, has said 'this is the worst the models will ever be' — a framing the host and guest treat as an operating truism for planning purposes, even though it now sounds cliché.
insights.speaker: host, quoting Kevin Weil (former OpenAI chief product officer)
insights.so_what: Reinforces the case for building product around a moving capability frontier rather than the present snapshot — a recurring justification inside OpenAI for aggressive forward-positioning.
insights.quote: This is the worst the models will ever be.

insights.claim: Seshan's mental model for the future of knowledge work is 'steering, not rowing': agents increasingly do the execution ('rowing') while humans direct at progressively higher levels of abstraction ('steering'), but a human's opinionated call about the desired direction remains necessary because the data alone doesn't dictate the choice.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A durable lens for identifying which roles/tasks stay human-anchored as agent autonomy increases — the steering layer, not the rowing layer, is where human headcount and judgment concentrate.
insights.quote: I do think that increasingly the future of work will look more like steering than rowing.

insights.claim: Because AI tools give everyone access to similar capability, human taste and opinion become the actual differentiator between products; Seshan compares this to fashion (functional clothes exist for everyone, but individual expression is what creates contrast) and cites a Patrick Collison-style view that software is more like filmmaking than real estate — budget/effort doesn't guarantee value, artistry and authorship do.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Supports a thesis that in a world of AI-parity tooling, competitive moats shift toward taste, positioning, and authored point of view rather than raw execution capability.
insights.quote: Software is not like real estate. You don't like put money in and get value out. It is a little bit more like film making where you can put a lot of money into a film but that doesn't guarantee that the film is successful or good.

insights.claim: Humans remain necessary primarily as the 'entity of accountability' for agent-produced work — someone must own whether an output is correct and high quality, which matters especially in regulated industries or contexts requiring a direct human interface.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Suggests durable human-in-the-loop demand specifically around accountability/compliance functions even as execution work is automated — relevant for where regulated-industry AI adoption will lag or require human sign-off layers.
insights.quote: I think humans will continue to be most valuable as a certainly as a um like an entity of accountability.

insights.claim: Human value also persists in creative authorship (deciding what to build and how it should feel) and in interpersonal team leadership (motivating and aligning colleagues) — neither is expected to be commoditized by models in the near term.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Points to authorship/vision-setting and people-management as the durable human skill categories to invest in as agent capability expands elsewhere.

themes.theme: Ambition as the New Competitive Edge

insights.claim: Seshan argues the people most effective with AI tools don't just automate rote tasks — they use AI to expand the total set of things they're capable of attempting, echoing the old 'unicorn' hire (PM who could also design and code) but now available to anyone via AI tooling.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A practical screen for evaluating individuals/teams: are they using AI to widen scope of ambition, or merely to speed up the same narrow tasks they already did? The former is the higher-leverage usage pattern.
insights.quote: The people that we see who are most effective at using AI tools don't simply use it to automate wrote tasks but use it to expand the set of things that they are capable of doing.

insights.claim: Seshan cites Patrick Collison's list of historically fast, ambitious projects (patrickcollison.com/fast) as a benchmark: since those projects were achievable with pre-AI tools, AI-augmented individuals and teams should now be capable of an exponential increase in similarly ambitious, quickly-executed projects — the limiting factor is simply remembering to try.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A useful benchmark/heuristic for judging whether a team's output pace matches what current tooling should allow, rather than what past-era norms suggest is fast.
insights.quote: If those fast projects were possible before with the capabilities we used to have, shouldn't we just see an exponential increase of the number of those types of unreasonably quickly and effectively executed things?

insights.claim: Seshan argues a core part of the modern PM role is actively 'elevating others' ambitions' — pushing colleagues to attempt bigger, faster, or larger-scale versions of what they initially proposed, referencing Tyler Cowen's observation that people underrate the value of simply asking someone to try a more ambitious or 10x-larger version of their plan.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Reframes PM value-add in AI-native orgs away from process/coordination and toward actively raising the ceiling of what teams believe is achievable — an evaluable leadership behavior.
insights.quote: Elevating others ambitions or reminding them of what's possible here is a huge part of the product management role.

insights.claim: OpenAI has an internal culture of using cultural 'memes' to enforce ambition and iteration speed as operating norms, rather than relying on formal process — three recurring internal phrases are 'is this maximally accelerated?', 'are you mainlining it yet?' (using your own product constantly), and 'feeling the AGI.'
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Gives investors/operators a window into OpenAI's actual internal accountability mechanisms for product velocity — informal cultural pressure substitutes for heavyweight process, which is a signal about how the org scales speed.
insights.quote: Is this maximally accelerated? Is totally a OpenAI meme. The other OpenAI meme that... we love to ask the team is like are you mainlining it yet which is like are you using this product all day every day to get your thing done.

themes.theme: Inside OpenAI: Founder-Led Culture and Codex's Rise vs. Claude Code

insights.claim: Contrary to her expectation of finding a centralized 'secret strategy' when she joined, Seshan found OpenAI to be unusually decentralized and founder-led internally — individuals are expected to act as founders of their own product area with minimal top-down direction, and internal thinking quickly becomes public product or public messaging.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Investor-relevant organizational signal: OpenAI's product strategy is highly distributed and legible externally (shows up fast in shipped product/messaging) rather than centrally planned and hidden — useful for reading OpenAI's public actions as genuine strategic signal, not noise.
insights.quote: I came into the company expecting that there was a treasure trove of like open AI secret strategy that I would be able to understand... and actually OpenAI is open.

insights.claim: Codex's recent surge in developer mindshare (a visible 'vibe shift' from Claude Code to Codex on Twitter over the prior few months) was not driven by a strategic pivot or major internal change, but by the existing team's sustained internal dogfooding and iteration — the operating model stayed the same and the external market simply caught up and started noticing.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Suggests Codex's competitive gains vs. Claude Code stem from compounding product-quality iteration rather than a single feature or marketing push — implies durability of the trend if the underlying iteration culture continues, rather than a one-off spike.
insights.quote: The team was always really focused on users, really focused on that iteration and it was merely... the market catching up that was the change... that process has not changed internally.

insights.claim: OpenAI's Codex desktop/app team operates with near-total independence: team members build and ship improvements on their own initiative when they notice gaps, test internally first, and only ship externally once it tests well with internal users — Seshan gives the team, not any AI capability, full credit for Codex's momentum.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Reinforces that Codex's edge is attributed to team execution/culture rather than a unique model advantage — a factor for competitors (including Anthropic/Claude Code) to weigh when assessing how replicable OpenAI's recent gains are.

themes.theme: Product Architecture: Merging Chat, Work, and Codex; Designing for Knowledge Work

insights.claim: OpenAI's stated near-term north star is to eliminate the current choice users face between ChatGPT chat mode, ChatGPT 'work' mode, and Codex — instead, a user will simply type their task in one box and the system will automatically select the right harness and model.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Signals OpenAI is moving toward a single unified agent product rather than maintaining separate coder-vs-consumer surfaces — competitors and enterprise buyers should expect UI/product consolidation, not permanent segmentation, from OpenAI's agent lineup.
insights.quote: Our north star here is that users do not need to make decisions between picking between all these different options... it will just pick the right harness. It'll pick the right model for you to be able to get that thing done.

insights.claim: ChatGPT's 'work' mode is, under the hood, literally Codex, with coding-specific UI elements (like the work-tree view) hidden and a knowledge-work-oriented interface shown instead — Codex users get identical underlying power without switching modes.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Clarifies OpenAI's actual technical architecture: one core agent engine (Codex) is being re-skinned for different audiences rather than maintaining separate agent stacks — relevant for assessing OpenAI's R&D leverage and product surface area.
insights.quote: In work mode that's where under the covers this is codeex.

insights.claim: OpenAI's own corporate finance team has adopted ChatGPT 'work' mode to build complex financial models that previously required deep manual expertise from a single specialist, turning that capability into something the whole team can execute and elevating the team's timeline and ambition.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A concrete internal case study of AI-driven skill democratization inside finance functions — a leading indicator for how corporate finance teams broadly may adopt agent tools for modeling work.

insights.claim: OpenAI's product philosophy has shifted from a pre-AI-era norm where 'polish was king' (every UI interaction had to be perfect before shipping, since speed didn't change outcomes much) to a norm where shipping fast to real users when you have strong conviction beats over-polishing — evidenced by the ChatGPT work launch, which caused initial user confusion but was rapidly iterated post-launch.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A generalizable lesson for AI-product teams: in fast-moving AI markets, iteration speed after launch is weighted above pre-launch polish, changing how investors should judge a rocky initial launch as a competence signal.
insights.quote: Done is better than perfect and we have so much more to do.

insights.claim: Cloud-agent usefulness depends as much on 'meat and potatoes' infrastructure — access to third-party systems and data (Slack, Google Docs, company databases), reliability, and cloud infra for long-running tasks — as on raw model intelligence; an agent isolated from a company's systems is compared to a locked-in employee with no tool access.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Reframes AI-agent competitive advantage as partly an integrations/infrastructure problem, not purely a model-capability problem — relevant for evaluating moats of agent startups that lack deep enterprise data-access partnerships.
insights.quote: A cloud agent that is similarly isolated will not be that effective.

insights.claim: Seshan identifies a fundamental product design difference between coding and knowledge work: coding output is verifiable via tests (pass/fail), but knowledge-work output (e.g., a financial model or deck) can't be trust-verified just by looking at the final numbers — trust requires visibility into the agent's process, inputs, reasoning, and citations along the way.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A key design principle for any AI product targeting knowledge work: in-progress transparency and citation visibility are necessary for adoption/trust, unlike coding agents where a pass/fail test suffices — a differentiator to check for in competing knowledge-work AI tools.
insights.quote: Coding is so output oriented that when you ask it to do a coding task, you can verify whether it did the task correctly or well via tests... But knowledge work is different in that I can't simply look at the deck in the end and see the numbers... and actually believe that.

insights.claim: Seshan distinguishes 'writing as thinking' (drafting a brief to work out a new idea or strategy — never to be automated, because the act of outlining/drafting/editing is how she refines her own thinking) from 'writing as reporting' (status updates, plans, announcements — which she happily automates with AI).
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A concrete, transferable rule for knowledge workers to prevent 'AI brain rot': automate the reporting layer, never outsource the thinking/drafting layer.
insights.quote: Writing is thinking is something I never will automate.

insights.claim: At OpenAI, the primary artifact used to persuade and drive decisions has shifted from long written docs to interactive mocks, working prototypes, and A/B test results ('mocks not docs, prototypes not docs') — reversing the Stripe-era culture where a viral internal brief was the main currency of ideas.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Signals that in fast-moving AI orgs, demoable/testable evidence beats written argument as the unit of internal persuasion — a cultural marker to look for when assessing whether a company's decision process matches AI-era speed.
insights.quote: I am way more on mocks not docs or prototypes not docs and if I have something that people can try and interact with or even better, I have like results where we tried this, we ran an AB, here's like the results.

insights.claim: To avoid AI eroding her own thinking, Seshan never lets a model write the first or final draft of a 'writing as thinking' document — she starts and ends the writing herself, using AI only in the middle to research, pull data, or pressure-test ideas — and holds herself to always reading/writing a document for at least as long as she expects its readers collectively to spend on it.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable personal discipline for knowledge workers worried about AI-driven skill atrophy in reasoning/writing.
insights.quote: At least for me, I start myself and I end myself. I might use AI in the middle to research specific elements or drop in some data... but start yourself and end yourself with a piece of writing and that doesn't deteriorate your thinking.

insights.claim: A career tip Seshan still follows: bring a document to roughly 70% completion before seeking buy-in feedback from stakeholders, then iterate it to 100% with them — because polished, 'finished-looking' drafts get less genuine pushback and improvement than deliberately rough ones with visible gaps.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A practical collaboration heuristic for getting higher-quality feedback on strategy documents/briefs — applicable to any team producing internal decision docs.
insights.quote: The right thing to always do is write a doc to 70% completion and then take it to the people that you need buy in from and get it from 70% to 100%.

insights.claim: Seshan argues that finding product-market fit is commonly treated as a 'dark art' driven by luck, but her time as an entrepreneur-in-residence at Sutter Hill Ventures (which incubated Snowflake, under partner Mike Spiser) convinced her it is instead a repeatable, codified internal playbook covering enterprise sales setup, product positioning, and founding-team construction.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: Suggests B2B company-building success is more process-replicable than commonly believed — relevant for evaluating incubator/venture-studio models (like Sutter Hill's) as a structurally repeatable source of outsized outcomes rather than one-off luck.
insights.quote: Sutter Hill is an iconic firm and is intentionally a very illegible firm... yet is somehow responsible for some of the most iconic successes that Silicon Valley has seen.

insights.claim: The key lesson Seshan took from Sutter Hill is that 'product marketing fit' — the narrative and positioning of a product — should be tested and refined before the product itself is fully built, by pitching the narrative to roughly 100 people and refining it, since she had previously underrated PMM as 'glue' work when it can actually be the deciding factor in a company's success.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable go-to-market sequencing insight: validate narrative/positioning ahead of product build via a pitch tour, rather than treating product marketing as a downstream activity — actionable for founders and product leaders.
insights.quote: Product market fit is sure important but actually I really underrated product marketing fit... you should go like pitch 100 people, figure out how to refine that pitch as much as possible... and only then go commit the... product shape.

insights.claim: Sutter Hill Ventures reportedly uses a proprietary internal recruiting tool called 'Reticle' that maps everyone the firm has interacted with plus each contact's top-10 best professional connections, giving it an unusually strong talent-sourcing pipeline for the companies it builds.
insights.speaker: Tara Seshan
insights.so_what: A specific, lesser-known mechanism behind Sutter Hill's repeated success — relevant color for anyone diligencing venture-studio/incubator models or Sutter Hill itself as a firm.
insights.quote: They have a secret tool called Reticle where they have a map of, you know, everyone in... that they've interacted with and the 10 best people that those people have interacted with.
